propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of the RAD decision confirming the RPD's rejection of refugee claims under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) that confirmed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting the applicants’ claim for refugee protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA or the Act].

propositions.text: Leave to apply for judicial review was granted under section 72 of the Act.
propositions.quote: Leave to apply for judicial review was granted under section 72 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of the RAD decision confirming the RPD's rejection of refugee claims, with leave granted under section 72 of IRPA.

propositions.text: Applicants are Iranian citizens alleging persecution by their government and fear of further persecution in Iran.
propositions.quote: The applicants are Iranian citizens who allege persecution by their government and a fear of further persecution in their country of nationality.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege persecution by Iranian government and fear further persecution in Iran.

propositions.text: Both RPD and RAD rejected claims due to applicants' lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: Both the RPD and the RAD rejected the claims on the grounds that the applicants were not credible.

propositions.text: A subpoena allegedly received by Mr. Baladi could partially corroborate persecution allegations but posed an evidentiary problem.
propositions.quote: An additional problem arose regarding a potentially significant piece of evidence, a subpoena that the applicant Mr. Baladi claims to have received, that could at least partially corroborate his allegations of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found applicants not credible and noted evidentiary issues with a subpoena potentially corroborating Mr. Baladi's claims.

propositions.text: Applicants arrived in Canada on temporary resident visas from Canadian Embassy in Türkiye on different dates.
propositions.quote: The applicants arrived in Canada on temporary resident visas obtained on different dates from the Embassy of Canada to Türkiye.

propositions.text: Ms. Reihani born 1960, Mr. Baladi born 1954; arrived together Nov 15, 2017; claimed refugee protection June 12, 2018.
propositions.quote: Ms. Reihani was born in 1960, and Mr. Baladi, in 1954. They arrived together on November 15, 2017, but did not claim refugee protection until June 12, 2018.

propositions.text: Both allegedly persecuted for political activities related to their jobs.
propositions.quote: Both were allegedly persecuted for political activities related in some way to their respective jobs.

paragraphs.summary: Court states applicants arrived on temporary visas in 2017, claimed refugee protection in 2018, alleging political persecution related to jobs.

propositions.text: Applicants chose not to speak directly before this Court about evidence found not credible.
propositions.quote: The applicants chose not to speak directly before this Court about the evidence they had submitted in support of their claims, which had been found not to be credible.

propositions.text: The evidence is described more fully to provide context.
propositions.quote: This evidence is worth describing more fully, to put the case into context.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes applicants did not speak directly about evidence found not credible and describes it for context.

propositions.text: Mr. Baladi criticized Iranian government at work; worked at Azmayesh Technical Company since 2003; interrogated by Heresat office; family opposed regime; brother disappeared after 2015 arrest.
propositions.quote: The Iranian authorities allegedly criticized Mr. Baladi for expressing his political opinion at work. His opinion of the current government was highly critical. His Basis of Claim Form [BOC Form] contains few details. It states that he had been working for a certain “Azmayesh Technical Company” since September 2003. He claims that the Heresat office interrogated him a few times over the years and that he belongs to a family that has been against the regime in place since the 1979 revolution. He also states that a brother of his disappeared after being arrested in November 2015.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Baladi alleges political criticism at work, interrogation, family opposition to regime, and brother's disappearance after 2015 arrest.

propositions.text: Mr. Baladi testified to participating in protest, uncertain about year, detained and beaten needing back surgery months later in 2016.
propositions.quote: Mr. Baladi testified before the RPD that he had participated in a protest against the regime. Surprisingly, he stated that he was not sure in what year and then at what point during 2015 he was detained and beaten so severely that he needed back surgery a number of months later, in 2016.

propositions.text: RPD transcript does not identify causes of Mr. Baladi's back problems; BOC Form states detention Oct 27, 2015, surgery Mar 11, 2016, recovery over next three months.
propositions.quote: I have read the transcript of the RPD hearing, and it does not appear to identify the causes of Mr. Baladi’s back problems. I note that the BOC Form states specifically that Mr. Baladi was detained on October 27, 2015, had surgery on March 11, 2016, and recovered from surgery over the three months that followed.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Baladi testified to protest participation and injury needing surgery; court notes transcript lacks cause details but BOC Form gives dates.

propositions.text: BOC Form describes Mr. Baladi's arrest Sept 10, 2017, detention, beating, interrogation, hospital stay, ransom payment, and subpoena for Islamic trial.
propositions.quote: The BOC Form goes on to describe Mr. Baladi’s arrest on September 10, 2017, and his detention. Mr. Baladi claims that he was arrested at work for remarks he had made to colleagues about the regime and that he was beaten while in detention. He was interrogated about his political activities and about his brother. He was not taken to a hospital until September 16, 2017. It was not until a ransom had been paid that he was released from hospital (where he was being held in custody) on condition that he appear at what the BOC Form refers to as an “Islamic trial”. Mr. Baladi claims that he was issued a subpoena. The translated version states that it was issued on October 23, 2017, for an appearance on November 8, 2017. The alleged offence is “participation in disturbing public order and disturbing public opinion”.

paragraphs.summary: BOC Form details Mr. Baladi's 2017 arrest, detention, beating, hospital stay, ransom, and subpoena for Islamic trial.

propositions.text: Mr. Baladi went to Ankara for Canadian visa Oct 4-8, 2017; visa issued Oct 18; left Iran Nov 15, 2017, missing Nov 8 court appearance; did not comply with subpoena.
propositions.quote: Following the attack in the first week of September, Mr. Baladi allegedly went to Ankara to obtain a temporary residence visa from the Embassy of Canada. He arrived in Türkiye on October 4, 2017, and returned to Iran on October 8. The visa was issued on October 18. The couple did not leave Iran for Canada until November 15, 2017, even though Mr. Baladi was scheduled to appear before the Islamic court on November 8, 2017. Mr. Baladi did not comply with the subpoena.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Baladi traveled to Ankara for visa, returned to Iran, visa issued, left Iran Nov 15, missing Nov 8 court date, did not comply with subpoena.

propositions.text: Ms. Reihani's situation unclear; BOC Form dated same as Mr. Baladi's states she was hired as teacher in 2000 and harassed at work.
propositions.quote: Ms. Reihani’s situation is not much clearer. In her BOC Form, which is dated the same as Mr. Baladi’s, she states that she was hired as a teacher in 2000 and was harassed at work.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Reihani states in BOC Form she was hired as teacher in 2000 and harassed at work.

propositions.text: Harassment started in 2015 after mosque built at school; Ms. Reihani summoned and ordered to attend midday prayer by mullah.
propositions.quote: It appears that the harassment started in 2015. A mosque had been built at the school where Ms. Reihani was teaching. A few months after the mosque was completed, she was summoned because she was not attending the midday prayer each day. A mullah ordered her to attend.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Reihani alleges harassment starting 2015 after mosque built; ordered to attend midday prayer by mullah.

propositions.text: Ms. Reihani told not to encourage girls resisting early marriage; insulted by Hezbollah principal; forced to sign undertaking.
propositions.quote: She was then told by the school office that she should not encourage girls to resist marrying at a young age and starting a family. Ms. Reihani states that she was insulted by the “Hezbollah principal” and forced to sign an undertaking to comply.

propositions.text: On Dec 1, 2016, Ms. Reihani asked students to write essays on human rights or society's openness; dispute arose Dec 4; principal accused her of provoking students.
propositions.quote: Some time later, on December 1, 2016, Ms. Reihani asked her students to write an essay on one of two topics: human rights or society’s openness to criticism. When the students were asked to discuss their essays on December 4, a dispute arose between two of them. The Hezbollah principal had to intervene. He accused Ms. Reihani of provoking the students.

propositions.text: Ms. Reihani detained 3 days, insulted, interrogated, beaten; house searched; dismissed from job.
propositions.quote: She was detained for three days, during which she claims to have been insulted, interrogated and beaten; in addition, her house was searched. Ms. Reihani was dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Reihani alleges school harassment, forced compliance, detention, abuse, house search, and dismissal after student essay dispute.

propositions.text: Ms. Reihani arrived in Canada Mar 21, 2017, where son lives; went to Türkiye Dec 22, 2016, for temporary residence visa, received Dec 29, 2016.
propositions.quote: Three months later, on March 21, 2017, she arrived in Canada, where a son of hers lives. In preparation for this trip, Ms. Reihani had gone to Türkiye on December 22, 2016, to obtain a temporary residence visa for Canada, which she received on December 29, 2016.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Reihani traveled to Türkiye for visa in Dec 2016, arrived in Canada Mar 2017 where son lives.

propositions.text: Ms. Reihani returned to Iran Sept 21, 2017; arrested at airport, detained one week, released on bail and undertaking; left Iran Nov 15, 2017 with Mr. Baladi.
propositions.quote: She returned to Iran on September 21, 2017. Before the RPD, Ms. Reihani stated that she returned because her husband was being detained. She was arrested at the airport upon her return, detained for one week and released on bail and on a written undertaking. No other details have been provided. Ms. Reihani and Mr. Baladi left Iran together on November 15, 2017, without incident. They have been in Canada ever since.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Reihani returned to Iran Sept 2017, arrested and detained one week, then left Iran Nov 2017 with Mr. Baladi.

propositions.text: RPD sought corroboration of applicants' story, questioned timing of Mr. Baladi's back injury and employment details.
propositions.quote: A review of the RPD hearing transcript clearly shows that the RPD was seeking corroboration of the applicants’ story. For example, the RPD wondered about Mr. Baladi’s back injury that required surgery several months after the incidents that allegedly caused the injury (the protest and Mr. Baladi’s subsequent arrest). Questions also arose about Mr. Baladi’s employment in 2016 and 2017.

propositions.text: Scarcity of details led to giving more weight to subpoena for Mr. Baladi's appearance on Nov 8, 2017.
propositions.quote: The relative scarcity of details resulted in the subpoena for Mr. Baladi’s appearance on November 8, 2017, being given more weight than it would probably have otherwise received.

paragraphs.summary: RPD sought corroboration, questioned injury timing and employment, and gave subpoena more weight due to scarce details.

propositions.text: Determinative issue for RPD and RAD was applicants' credibility.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue for both the RPD and the RAD was whether the applicants’ stories were credible.

propositions.text: This judicial review concerns only the RAD's decision.
propositions.quote: Of course, this is an application for judicial review of the RAD’s decision only.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-makers focused on applicants' credibility; judicial review concerns only RAD's decision.

propositions.text: RPD considered subpoena copy unreliable as Mr. Baladi did not produce original.
propositions.quote: From the outset, the RAD noted that the RPD considered the copy of the subpoena to be unreliable, especially since Mr. Baladi had made no effort to produce the original.

propositions.text: Subpoena corroborates incident involving Mr. Baladi but was emailed by his daughter, not original document.
propositions.quote: The subpoena appears to corroborate an incident involving Mr. Baladi. Without it, there is little direct evidence to support the allegations, apart from the applicants’ testimony. There was some confusion about the subpoena at the RPD hearing. It was eventually established that the document filed (P-13) was in fact a document that had been emailed to Mr. Baladi by his daughter in Iran.

propositions.text: RPD drew negative inference from lack of documentation on back surgery allegedly due to 2015 abuse.
propositions.quote: The RPD also drew a negative inference from the lack of documentation on the back surgery allegedly required as a result of abuse by the authorities in 2015.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found subpoena copy unreliable, noted it was emailed by daughter, and negatively inferred from lack of back surgery documentation.

propositions.text: Ms. Reihani claimed detention and abuse Dec 2016 but left Iran three months later without difficulty.
propositions.quote: In addition, Ms. Reihani claims she was detained and abused in December 2016, yet she had no difficulty leaving Iran three months later to visit her son in Canada.

propositions.text: RPD considered applicants' ability to leave Iran undermined their credibility regarding past and future abuse.
propositions.quote: The RAD points out that the RPD considered the credibility of the applicants’ account of past and potential future abuse to be undermined by their ability to leave Iran unhindered by the authorities.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Ms. Reihani's ability to leave Iran undermined credibility of abuse claims.

propositions.text: RAD dismissed appeal due to applicants' credibility issues, raised own credibility questions.
propositions.quote: The RAD therefore dismissed the appeal because the applicants’ credibility was undermined. In fact, the RAD raised its own credibility issues and questioned the applicants.

propositions.text: RAD questioned number of Ms. Reihani's detentions, found unclear.
propositions.quote: The questions were about the number of times Ms. Reihani claimed she had been detained, which seemed unclear to the RAD.

propositions.text: RAD noted letter from son suggested Ms. Reihani planned return to Iran since August 2017, not prompted by husband's detention.
propositions.quote: Although Ms. Reihani testified that she returned to Iran because her husband had been arrested there, the RAD noted that a letter from her son suggested she had been planning to return to Iran since August 2017. Therefore, it would not have been her husband’s detention that prompted her to return to Iran.

propositions.text: National Documentation Package amended with new info on Iran entry/exit, possibly undermining applicants' credibility.
propositions.quote: Lastly, the National Documentation Package had been amended since the RPD decision, and it contained new information on entering and leaving Iran that might undermine the applicants’ credibility.

propositions.text: RAD noted strict controls on people like applicants, casting doubt on their claims; they should have encountered problems entering/leaving Iran if claims true.
propositions.quote: The RAD noted that there were strict controls on people such as the applicants, which cast doubt on the applicants’ claims. Assuming that the claims were true, the applicants should have encountered problems entering and leaving Iran.

paragraphs.summary: RAD dismissed appeal due to credibility issues, questioned detention claims, planning of return, and noted strict Iranian controls.

propositions.text: RAD found applicants not credible after independent review.
propositions.quote: Having completed its independent review, the RAD found that the applicants were not credible.

propositions.text: Applicants alleged RPD failed to act impartially based on its interpretation of evidence.
propositions.quote: It rejected the allegation that the RPD had failed to act impartially. This allegation was based on the RPD’s interpretation of the applicants’ evidence.

propositions.text: RPD weighing evidence and drawing conclusions is not bias.
propositions.quote: However, the very role of the RPD is to weigh evidence and draw conclusions. To do so is not to be biased.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found applicants not credible, rejected bias allegation against RPD, stating weighing evidence is not bias.

propositions.text: RAD questioned if applicants could have left Iran as claimed given strict controls and their punishable activities
propositions.quote: the RAD did not find the applicants’ allegations to be credible, especially since their activities were considered by the authorities to be punishable by detention and release on an undertaking

propositions.text: If claims true, doubtful applicants could enter and leave Iran easily
propositions.quote: If the applicants’ claims were true, it would be doubtful that they could have entered and left Iran so easily

propositions.text: Mr. Baladi allegedly failed to comply with subpoena, making his departure less likely
propositions.quote: Mr. Baladi allegedly failed to comply with a subpoena... made it less likely that he could have left the country a week later

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found applicants' claims not credible due to strict Iranian controls and Mr. Baladi's failure to comply with subpoena, questioning their departure timing.

propositions.text: Applicants' claimed reprisals made it implausible they could leave Iran given harsh treatment and political interest
propositions.quote: It was not credible that the applicants were able to leave Iran if their allegations of harsh treatment were true

propositions.text: RAD made cautious implausibility finding based on clear and well-founded evidence
propositions.quote: The RAD made its finding of implausibility cautiously, on the basis of evidence that it considered to be clear and well-founded

paragraphs.summary: RAD found it implausible applicants could leave Iran given harsh reprisals, basing this cautious finding on clear evidence.

propositions.text: RAD doubted subpoena's authenticity due to appearance and lack of original or certified copy
propositions.quote: The RAD also had doubts

paragraphs.summary: RAD doubted subpoena's authenticity due to document appearance and absence of original or certified copy.

propositions.text: RAD requested RPD Copy of subpoena but it was missing from record, presumed sent to Minister
propositions.quote: it was presumed that the copy of the Appellants’ Record containing the RPD Copy of the subpoena was inadvertently sent to the Minister

propositions.text: RAD Registry's efforts to obtain RPD Copy from Minister were unsuccessful
propositions.quote: The RAD Registry subsequently made efforts to obtain the RPD Copy from the Minister, which were unfortunately unsuccessful

propositions.text: RAD found RAD Copy showed same issues as RPD Copy, no meaningful advantage to RPD Copy
propositions.quote: I do not find that the RPD had any meaningful advantage in reviewing the RPD Copy

propositions.text: RAD not satisfied subpoena copy was authentic on balance of probabilities due to appearance and failure to produce certified copy
propositions.quote: I am not satisfied that the document provided is a true copy of an authentic subpoena, on a balance of probabilities

propositions.text: Allegation of outstanding subpoena at departure not credible; matter warrants referral back to RAD
propositions.quote: I find that the allegation that the Principal Appellant was subject to an outstanding subpoena at the time of his departure is not credible. I will come back to this because I believe that it warrants referring the matter back to the RAD

paragraphs.summary: RAD found subpoena copy not authentic and the allegation of outstanding subpoena not credible, recommending referral back to RAD.

propositions.text: RAD found inconsistency in Mr. Baladi's employer info and rejected explanation of fictitious documentation
propositions.quote: This explanation was not accepted. Three reasons were given

propositions.text: No evidence a facilitator obtained evidence; Mr. Baladi testified to working for both companies
propositions.quote: there was no evidence that a facilitator had obtained that evidence

propositions.text: Failure to mention Tasalsol Nasb Co in refugee claim noted as problematic
propositions.quote: he failed to mention it in his claim for refugee protection in Canada

paragraphs.summary: RAD rejected Mr. Baladi's employer explanation due to lack of evidence and contradictions, noting failure to mention employer in claim.

propositions.text: RAD noted inconsistency in Ms. Reihani's detention evidence and included 2015 summons for missing prayers
propositions.quote: the RAD noted an inconsistency in the evidence as to the number of times she had been detained

paragraphs.summary: RAD noted inconsistencies in Ms. Reihani's detention evidence including a 2015 summons for missed prayers.

propositions.text: RAD found letters of support had little probative value as they corroborated harassment but not core claims
propositions.quote: the letters had little probative value because they tended to corroborate reprimands and harassment but not what was at the heart of the applicants’ claim

propositions.text: One letter included new unverified allegation of Ms. Reihani's travel to save her life
propositions.quote: One of the letters even included a completely new allegation that Ms. Reihani had travelled from city to city before leaving for Canada to save her life

propositions.text: This evidence had little probative value
propositions.quote: This evidence has little probative value

paragraphs.summary: RAD found letters of support had little probative value and included unverified new allegations, thus weak evidence.

propositions.text: Disappearance of Mr. Baladi’s brother irrelevant as not linked to his activities
propositions.quote: it is simply not relevant because his disappearance was never linked to Mr. Baladi’s activities

propositions.text: No specific fear based on ethnicity alleged, only fear of government opposition
propositions.quote: no specific allegation was ever made of a fear based on ethnicity; the applicants merely alleged a fear of the government they oppose

paragraphs.summary: RAD found brother's disappearance irrelevant and no specific ethnic fear alleged, only fear of government.

propositions.text: RAD concluded major concerns on applicants’ credibility and allegations; applicants try all angles on review
propositions.quote: the RAD concluded that there were major concerns regarding the applicants’ credibility and the quality of their allegations, and now, on judicial review, the applicants are trying every angle possible

propositions.text: Concerns raised can be dismissed but subpoena issue requires referral back to RAD for reconsideration
propositions.quote: all the concerns raised with respect to the RAD’s decision can be easily dismissed... it is both necessary and prudent to refer the matter back to the RAD for reconsideration

propositions.text: New evidence filed by applicants and respondent in 2022
propositions.quote: new evidence was filed by the applicants on January 26, 2022, and by the respondent on February 10 and March 22, 2022

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD's credibility concerns dismissible but subpoenas issue warrants referral back; new evidence filed in 2022.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is standard for credibility issues per Vavilov
propositions.quote: Reasonableness has been the presumptive standard since Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov

propositions.text: Subpoena loss raises procedural fairness issue requiring correctness standard review
propositions.quote: It calls for the standard of correctness... where the reviewing court must be satisfied that procedural fairness has been met

propositions.text: Reviewing court owes no particular deference to administrative tribunal on procedural fairness
propositions.quote: the reviewing court owes no particular deference to the administrative tribunal

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness applies to credibility; subpoena loss raises procedural fairness needing correctness standard; no deference on fairness.

propositions.text: Applicants present three arguments: inconsistent analysis, premature non-credibility finding, and natural justice breach from subpoena loss
propositions.quote: The applicants have presented three arguments to this Court: (a)... (b)... (c)...

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue inconsistent analysis, premature non-credibility finding, and natural justice breach from subpoena loss.

propositions.text: RAD erred by not accepting corroborative letters, leading to premature non-credibility finding
propositions.quote: The applicants submit that the RAD erred by failing to accept corroborative evidence consisting of letters of support

propositions.text: Unreasonable to find non-credibility without considering corroborative evidence, citing Cheema and Jiang
propositions.quote: it is “unreasonable to reach a finding of non-credibility without considering corroborative evidence

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD erred by dismissing corroborative letters and making premature non-credibility finding, citing cases.

propositions.text: Corroborative evidence confirms other evidence and must be considered before credibility assessment
propositions.quote: Corroborative evidence is independent evidence that confirms other evidence

propositions.text: Assessing credibility before corroboration and then rejecting evidence as not credible is circular and illogical
propositions.quote: It goes against common sense to assess credibility before considering corroborating evidence and then reject the evidence on the basis that it is not credible because the applicant is not credible

paragraphs.summary: Court explains corroborative evidence must be considered before credibility; rejecting it after credibility is circular and illogical.

propositions.text: RAD gave letters little weight due to low probative value, not due to applicants' credibility
propositions.quote: The letters in support of the applicants were given little weight because of their low intrinsic probative value

propositions.text: RAD's assessment of letters' probative value was open to fact-finder and not unreasonable
propositions.quote: It was open to the master of the facts to make these assessments, and it is hard to see how they would be unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably assessed letters as low probative value, not rejecting them due to applicants' credibility.

propositions.text: Applicants' attack on RAD's justification is without merit; RAD addressed grounds raised
propositions.quote: In my opinion, this ground of attack is without merit. The decision is justified on the basis of the issues raised

propositions.text: Applicants' memorandum focused on undermined credibility; RAD dealt with that issue on appeal
propositions.quote: It focuses on undermined credibility... The RAD can hardly be faulted for dealing with the grounds of appeal brought before it

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects applicants' claim that RAD's decision lacked justification, noting RAD addressed credibility grounds raised.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD erred in law applying implausibility test regarding travel and subpoena
propositions.quote: The applicants submit that the RAD erred in law in applying the implausibility test

propositions.text: RAD requested submissions on new evidence about Iran's entry/exit controls and travel bans
propositions.quote: the National Documentation Package had been amended... requesting submissions regarding entering and leaving Iran

propositions.text: RAD found it implausible applicants left Iran easily given travel bans after alleged subpoena non-compliance
propositions.quote: It was therefore not plausible that they left only one week after Mr. Baladi allegedly failed to appear at the Islamic court

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD erred applying implausibility test; RAD found departure implausible given new evidence on travel bans.

propositions.text: Court finds RAD applied correct legal test and exercised due caution on implausibility
propositions.quote: I do not agree that the RAD failed to apply the appropriate legal test... The RAD did not err in law as alleged. It exercised due caution

propositions.text: Applicants bear burden to show error of law; review not a treasure hunt for error per Vavilov
propositions.quote: the burden is on the applicants to show that an error of law occurred... and that the review is not a treasure hunt for error

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD applied correct implausibility test and applicants failed to show legal error as required by Vavilov.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with applicants' claim that RAD made contradictory argument
propositions.quote: Somewhat in the same vein, the applicants argue that the RAD made a contradictory argument in the decision it rendered. I disagree

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects applicants' claim that RAD made contradictory argument.

propositions.text: Applicants say RAD contradicted itself on reasons for travel ban: arrest/release/failure to comply vs political involvement
propositions.quote: the applicants are submitting that the contradiction arises from the RAD’s statement...

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD contradicted itself on travel ban reasons: legal issues vs political involvement.

propositions.text: Court finds no contradiction; legal problems and political involvement are consistent reasons for travel ban
propositions.quote: It is hard to see where the contradiction lies... The problems with the law, which stemmed from political activities, and the travel ban are consistent

propositions.text: Reasons could be clearer but perfection not required
propositions.quote: The reasons for decision could be clearer, but perfection is not the goal

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no contradiction in RAD's reasons; legal and political reasons for travel ban consistent; clarity not perfection.

propositions.text: The RAD found the applicants' account not credible because documentary evidence showed they could not leave Iran easily.
propositions.quote: Their account on its own, without further evidence, was not considered to be credible because documentary evidence indicated that people such as the applicants could not leave so easily.

propositions.text: The RAD concluded the applicants' account is not credible.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the account is not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the applicants' account not credible because documentary evidence showed they could not leave Iran easily, concluding the account is not credible.

propositions.text: The existence of a subpoena for November 8, 2017, is significant to the disputed story about leaving Iran.
propositions.quote: the existence of a subpoena for an appearance on November 8, 2017, is significant.

propositions.text: The story would be stronger if an order to appear before an Islamic court was issued.
propositions.quote: The story would be stronger if an order to appear before an Islamic court was in fact issued.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the subpoena's existence is significant and would strengthen the applicants' story if issued.

propositions.text: Whether the subpoena is reliable evidence that Mr. Baladi was targeted by the regime.
propositions.quote: The subpoena could be evidence that Mr. Baladi was targeted by the regime.

propositions.text: Whether leaving Iran despite the subpoena undermines the applicants' credibility.
propositions.quote: it is also possible that being able to leave the country without difficulty despite the subpoena does not undermine the applicants’ credibility.

propositions.text: The RAD found the subpoena copy unreliable and drew a negative inference from the missing original subpoena.
propositions.quote: The RAD drew a negative inference from the fact that an original subpoena was not produced (RAD decision at para 35).

propositions.text: The RAD concluded the copy raised doubts about authenticity and found the allegation of an outstanding subpoena not credible.
propositions.quote: I am not satisfied that the document provided is a true copy of an authentic subpoena, on a balance of probabilities... I find that the allegation that the Principal Appellant was subject to an outstanding subpoena at the time of his departure is not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the subpoena copy unreliable, doubted its authenticity, and rejected the allegation of an outstanding subpoena as not credible.

propositions.text: The subpoena is important documentary evidence supporting the applicants' assertions beyond their testimony alone.
propositions.quote: The importance of the subpoena seems obvious. It is documentary evidence that gives more weight to the applicants’ assertions than does their testimony alone.

propositions.text: Applicants claim the original subpoena was filed with the RAD and then lost, making RAD's conclusions invalid.
propositions.quote: the applicants claiming that the original subpoena had been filed with the RAD and then lost. If this is true, the RAD’s conclusions are invalid and the entire case must be reconsidered

propositions.text: The subpoena affects credibility and the conclusion that applicants would not have left Iran easily.
propositions.quote: the subpoena is important not only for the conclusion that the applicants would not have left Iran (which they obviously did) but also for the very allegations that affect the credibility of the applicants

paragraphs.summary: The subpoena is important evidence; applicants claim it was filed and lost, which would invalidate RAD's conclusions affecting credibility and departure from Iran.

propositions.text: The Court requested notes to clarify the subpoena situation after the hearing.
propositions.quote: at the end of the hearing, the Court requested notes to clarify the situation.

propositions.text: The RPD hearing transcript confirmed the subpoena copy was emailed by the applicants' daughter.
propositions.quote: the RPD hearing transcript confirmed that the copy of the subpoena before the RPD was a document emailed by the applicants’ daughter.

propositions.text: Applicants filed affidavits after the hearing explaining previously unexplained matters.
propositions.quote: The applicants filed affidavits after the hearing before this Court. These affidavits explain what had so far remained unexplained.

paragraphs.summary: The Court requested clarification; the RPD transcript showed the subpoena copy was emailed by the applicants' daughter; applicants filed affidavits explaining.

propositions.text: Counsel for applicants filed an original subpoena with the RAD, which was lost by the department.
propositions.quote: counsel for the applicants before the RAD filed an “original” subpoena with the RAD... a Department of Citizenship and Immigration official wrote... apologizing for... an item... apparently never delivered.

propositions.text: The letter confirms a document was lost; affidavits describe the problem more clearly.
propositions.quote: The letter... confirms that a document was lost; the affidavits made on behalf of the applicants describe the problem more clearly.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants' counsel filed an original subpoena with the RAD, which was lost; a letter and affidavits confirm and explain the loss.

propositions.text: Applicants' niece assisted with the claim, observed the RPD hearing, and noted focus on the subpoena.
propositions.quote: their niece... states that she assisted the applicants in their refugee protection claim; she was an observer at the RPD hearing and noticed the focus on the subpoena.

propositions.text: Mailing the original subpoena from Iran was inadvisable; an uncle carried it out and sent it to counsel.
propositions.quote: mailing it from Iran was inadvisable because it could be intercepted and seized... This was done by an uncle... who managed to get the so-called “original document” out... sent the “original document” to counsel

paragraphs.summary: Applicants' niece assisted and observed the hearing; mailing subpoena was risky, so an uncle carried it out and sent it to counsel.

propositions.text: Counsel realized the importance of providing the original subpoena and received it from the niece in January 2020.
propositions.quote: He states that he realized after the RPD hearing that it was important to provide the “original subpoena from Iran” rather than the emailed copy. He received the original subpoena in January 2020 from the applicants’ niece

paragraphs.summary: Counsel realized the original subpoena's importance and received it from the niece in January 2020.

propositions.text: The original document was filed in the appeal record after clerical return by the RAD.
propositions.quote: The “original document” was filed in support of the memorandum in the appeal record after the record was returned to him by the RAD for what appears to be clerical reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The original document was filed in the appeal record after the RAD returned it for clerical reasons.

propositions.text: The record has been lost since then; counsel describes efforts to locate it and asserts the original subpoena was filed.
propositions.quote: The record has been lost since then. Counsel describes discussions... He states that he filed “the original”... and argues it was filed in the appeal record before the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The record was lost; counsel describes efforts to locate it and asserts the original subpoena was filed with the RAD.

propositions.text: Mr. Baladi identified the document received by his niece as the original subpoena issued in Iran.
propositions.quote: He states that he identified the document received by his niece “as being the original subpoena issued in Iran”

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Baladi identified the document received by his niece as the original subpoena issued in Iran.

propositions.text: Respondent's affiant handled the record but had nothing to add about the loss.
propositions.quote: The respondent called an affiant who... stated merely that she had handled the record. The affiant had nothing to add regarding the loss of record.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent's affiant handled the record but had no information about the loss.

propositions.text: Respondent disputes breach of natural justice and notes new evidence was not requested under subsection 110(4) IRPA.
propositions.quote: The respondent’s submissions do not dispute that the record was lost. They do dispute that there was a breach of natural justice... the new evidence was not the subject of a request under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Respondent claims RAD's determination that applicants failed to submit original subpoena and explain why is well-founded.
propositions.quote: the RAD’s determination that the applicants failed to submit the ‘original’ subpoena obtained from Iran and failed to explain why is well-founded.

propositions.text: The court finds the respondent ignores that the respondent lost the original subpoena information.
propositions.quote: this ignores the fact that the respondent forwarded and lost the information about the original.

propositions.text: Applicants tried to provide the original subpoena but were unable due to administrative oversight not their fault.
propositions.quote: The applicants tried to provide the “original” subpoena, but were unable to because of an administrative oversight for which they cannot be held responsible.

propositions.text: It is now established that an original subpoena exists and was produced, which disposes of respondent's submissions.
propositions.quote: there is no longer any doubt that an “original” does exist and that it was produced... this is sufficient to dispose of the respondent’s submissions.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent disputes breach and original subpoena submission; court finds respondent lost the original, applicants not at fault, and original subpoena exists and was produced.

propositions.text: Respondent challenges affidavits but has not cross-examined affiants.
propositions.quote: The respondent reviewed the applicants’ affidavits and is challenging the assertions made. However, the respondent has not cross-examined the affiants.

propositions.text: Respondent argues court need not accept everything in affidavits without reasons.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues that the Court does not have to accept everything in an affidavit. Still, the Court should have reasons before it does so.

propositions.text: Court finds respondent should have sought explanation from affiants but did not.
propositions.quote: If the respondent has issues with some of the affiants’ statements, it should have sought an explanation from the affiants... That was not done.

propositions.text: Respondent's criticisms relate to the lost document's originality but no cross-examination was done.
propositions.quote: Many of the respondent’s criticisms relate... to the question of how the lost document was an original subpoena. The respondent has chosen not to challenge by cross-examination what was stated under oath.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent challenges affidavits but did not cross-examine; court finds respondent should have sought explanations but did not.

propositions.text: Respondent argues applicants were not prevented from submitting evidence despite lost record.
propositions.quote: the applicants were not prevented from submitting their evidence.

propositions.text: Court finds this argument contradicts RAD decision emphasizing subpoena's importance.
propositions.quote: This seems to contradict the very contents of the RAD decision. The original subpoena has become a potentially pivotal piece of evidence.

propositions.text: It is not the reviewing court's role to supplant the administrative tribunal's role in reviewing merits.
propositions.quote: it is not a reviewing court’s place to supplant the administrative tribunal’s role in reviewing a case on its merits.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues applicants were not prevented from submitting evidence; court finds this contradicts RAD and notes court cannot supplant tribunal's role.

propositions.text: Respondent states applicants failed to indicate which subpoena element would be analyzed differently if original.
propositions.quote: the applicants failed to indicate which element of the subpoena would have been analyzed differently had it been the original subpoena from Iran.

propositions.text: Court finds respondent misunderstands RAD's reasons; existence of subpoena is key to credibility.
propositions.quote: The statement suggests a possible misunderstanding of the RAD’s reasons for decision... the very existence a subpoena that is important.

propositions.text: If subpoena exists, it supports applicants being targeted and affects credibility.
propositions.quote: If a subpoena exists, it can no longer be argued that it is not credible that they are being targeted by the government.

propositions.text: Negative inference from missing original subpoena no longer holds given its existence.
propositions.quote: The negative inference drawn by the RAD from the fact that the original subpoena was not produced no longer holds.

propositions.text: Applicants were not afforded procedural fairness commensurate with evidence and consequences of negative decision.
propositions.quote: the applicants were not afforded the measure of procedural fairness commensurate with the evidence in question and the consequences that a negative decision would have on them

paragraphs.summary: Respondent claims applicants failed to specify subpoena impact; court finds subpoena existence key, negative inference invalid, and procedural fairness lacking.

propositions.text: The matter should be referred back to the RAD for redetermination with the subpoena accepted as authentic fact.
propositions.quote: the matter should be referred back to the RAD for redetermination... its authenticity must now be accepted as fact before the RAD.

propositions.text: The appeal must be reconsidered on the basis that the authentic subpoena is in the appeal record and not disputed.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the appeal must be reconsidered, on the basis that the authentic subpoena is in the applicants’ appeal record. The authenticity of the subpoena is not to be disputed.

paragraphs.summary: Court orders referral back to RAD for redetermination accepting subpoena authenticity as fact and reconsidering appeal accordingly.

propositions.text: Applicants may argue before RAD to admit authentic subpoena as new evidence; RAD may hold oral hearing.
propositions.quote: The applicants may argue before the RAD that the authentic subpoena is available (virtually) and that it should be admitted as new evidence on appeal to the RAD under the IRPA. The RAD may choose to hold an oral hearing if permitted under the Act.

propositions.text: The process will follow its course and evidence will be reassessed.
propositions.quote: The process will follow its course and the evidence will be reassessed.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants may seek to admit subpoena as new evidence before RAD, which may hold hearing; evidence will be reassessed accordingly.

propositions.text: Judicial review application is allowed; subpoena's importance warrants new proceeding with authenticity accepted.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed. The importance of the subpoena issued to Mr. Baladi warrants a new proceeding before the RAD, with the authenticity of the subpoena concerning Mr. Baladi being accepted as fact.

paragraphs.summary: Judicial review is allowed; subpoena's importance warrants new RAD proceeding with authenticity accepted as fact.

propositions.text: Parties will return to initial appeal stage; new panel will hear appeal and make new determination.
propositions.quote: The parties will return to the initial stage of the appeal, and a new panel will be called upon to hear the appeal and make a new determination.

paragraphs.summary: Parties return to initial appeal stage; new panel will hear appeal and make new determination.

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance arises from the highly exceptional circumstances of this case.
propositions.quote: Given the highly exceptional circumstances of this case and the fact that the issues arise from the particular evidence in question, there is no serious question of general importance which ought to be certified.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed and the matter is referred back to a differently constituted panel of the RAD.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed. The matter is referred back for redetermination by a differently constituted panel of the RAD.

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance is certified under section 74 of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: There is no serious question of general importance to certify under section 74 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious question of general importance, allows the judicial review, and refers the matter back to a different RAD panel, declining certification under IRPA s.74.
